Those enemies with whom you once shed blood,
And your wish will fall into your hands.’
So spoke the dervish,
Taking my hand and drawing me close.
While I lay sleeping in my dream,
He startled me with a sudden shove.
My snoring stopped,
And my eyes flew wide as scattered flour.
I swiftly awoke from my dream,
My heart pounding like a horse,
For I had received tidings from the unseen.
My dear heart rejoiced,
And I wondered where the famed champion Kuyaly
Had been born,
And in what land her mother
Had given birth to that champion.
He could traverse a horse’s whole course;
Across the entire wide world,
He could roam in twelve days.
He knew seventy different tongues
And traveled freely over the earth.
So to Agybai, son of the Argyn khan,
The interpreter of that gray wolf,
I gave six swift horses
And a letter small as my palm,
Dressed him in a fine gray robe,
And mounted him on the swift camel.
To discover whether she was indeed
The destined bride of the noble lion
And return with certain knowledge,
I mounted him on the swift camel
And sent him journeying across the earth,
Quenching his thirst with sunshine,
Feeding him provisions rich as külaзык,
And clothing him in flowered silk,
While the mount grew stronger with each day’s ride.
Mounting him on the swift camel,
I sent Agybai on his way.
Without letting a single soul know,
Without giving any person an inkling,
Without the gossipers learning of it,
Without even the dust-bearing wind knowing,
I spread out abundant wealth and countless livestock—
Pure gold coins and precious stones—
Before Agybai,
Saying, “Take these as gifts.”
Displaying all my riches,
I made poor Agybai,
From that time until this,
Grasp the holy Quran.
I had him pierce a steel bullet,
Chew a loaf of gray-wheat bread,
And swear ninety varied and solemn oaths
That he would reveal nothing.
I made him lick the sword’s edge
And swear upon immediate death.
“My dear Agybai,
When you mount Endik, rein in his mouth;
Among witless people, restrain your tongue.
The sorrowful words I have spoken
Have a name heard, but no visible form.
Kuyaly, daughter of Kaiypchal,
Is destined to be my daughter-in-law,
My daughter-in-law for the world hereafter,
The dark eye of prosperity.
My son Semetey,
A lion surpassing all heroes,
Is the one she shall marry.
She is the Night of Destiny itself.
My dear Agybai,
Learn where the champion Kuyaly
Sows her grain;
Learn her lineage, worthy of a father,
And the land where her clan took root.
If you return knowing this, Agybai,
We shall arrange the match while we live:
Setting aside many thousands of mares,
Separating double-humped camels,
And allotting abundant wealth and livestock,
With a white kerchief bound upon the brow,
We shall drive all the livestock
To seal the marriage pact.
Let us place a halter around her neck
And fetters upon her feet;
Let us hold a feast beneath the open sky
And take that proud one
To be our daughter-in-law.
Bringing her into the white palace,
We shall serve abundant kinds of sweet food.
Made Ajybay drink,
Dressed him in Jekeyboz,
And mounted Ajybay
On the dark swift camel that flew like a cloud,
Outstripping the wind,
For I had conceived a wondrous plan,
And was carrying out that wonder.
To poor Ajybay
I commanded, “Find the warrior maiden,”
Thus giving him my order.
“Range across the breadth of the earth,
Traverse the whole world,
Reach and explore it all.
Through the world’s four corners
Travel everywhere,
And of all the created earth
Leave not one place unsearched.
Visit the five corners of the known world,
Circle them five times,
And discover the known abode
Of that valiant, ill-fated maiden.
If by chance you return without seeing her,
Then may you behold the land of no return,
And cease to walk among the living.
If you are truly a formidable man,
If you, Ajybay, are a lion,
Discover the ancestry
And lineage of that hapless one.
If you will not go and search the earth,
If you ignore your sister-in-law’s courteous words
And fail to find the warrior maiden,
Your words will become mere boasting;
You have received such wealth,
And it will bring you shame.
Your words will sound frivolous,
Disgraceful talk will fall
Upon my unhappy self.
I was the mother of the teeming people,
The fruit of the lofty plane tree,
Their queen and khan’s lady.
You, dear pilgrim, were the people’s mediator,
A unifier among the multitude.
You were a man of surpassing wisdom,
The finest of the Argyn khans,
The khan of the forty companions.
Sharp-sighted while alive,
Clear in answering an enemy’s words,
May your road be open when you journey;
While you live, ride forth against the foe.
The sun shone beside your moon,
You knew seventy kinds of speech,
You sharpened the honored tongue
And spoke eloquently among the people.
When hardship came, you found a way,
And struck a bloodthirsty enemy
With all the authority of a khan.
Great orator, cultivator of wisdom,
You were the eye of swift-footed heroes.
Sage who cultivated wisdom,
You were the very master of great knowledge.
Heed these precious words:
Learn some news
Of that formidable warrior maiden.
If you fail to learn the truth,
Do not appear before my eyes,
And do not approach me.
May poison enter your blood,
Should Ajybay fail to return
From the city of Jangdüng-bash.
I, unfortunate Kanykey,
Was once a discerning soul.
What would come and what would pass,
What would be and what would not,
Joy and suffering,
Calamity and death—
There was once a naked child
Upon my right shoulder,
Beneath my ten locks of hair,
Who foretold them at once.
Now he has given this sign:
My son Semetey,
Born of his father, generous Manas,
Was destined to surpass him.
For that son of mine,
Upon my child’s brow,
Three marriages were written.
Let me tell of the first two:
When cruel disaster struck,
My dear son, only six months old,
Fled to the city of the Kara Khan
And wandered there in exile,
Until my noble child grew up.
Among the sights of Bukhara,
He matured as an orphan,
Joining in the affairs of the land,
And when he reached twelve years,
He married Shaatemir’s daughter Chachykey,
Pouring out treasures for her raven hair
And holding a feast for the gathered people.
Willful, foolish,
Swaggering infidel,
Restless madcap of surly temper,
In the end you did as you pleased.
The moon waned and the days passed;
Afterward he met
Aichürök, Akun’s daughter.
She stole away his falcon
And wore down his racehorse;
She became his precious wife,
A cultivator of wisdom whose speech was honey—
No other human could equal her!
Let us speak of the third:
Kuyaly, daughter of Kayypchal,
Was his third wife.
The twenty-year-old warrior maiden—
I, unfortunate woman, had hoped
She might come into my hands.
I camped beside the river,
And loved, not my son,
But my daughter-in-law herself.
The moon rose and the days passed,
And many days went by.
Then Ajybay of the Argyn khans
Brought me certain news.
When Ajybay finally came,
Sixty ladies and eighty maidens
Went out to meet him.
Speaking softly yet firmly,
Ajybay of the Argyn khans
Then began his account:
“Through the world’s four corners,
O senior wife who bore a prince,
I traveled four full circuits.
Through Medina’s five quarters
I traveled five full circuits.
I saw lands of countless kinds,
I witnessed many astonishing things,
And saw peoples of surpassing wonder.
Where the women were human and the men were dogs—
Such marvels have I seen.
Every creature that was born
I saw matched with its heart’s desire.
From savage waters to wondrous steeds,
Every strange and ill-starred being,
I saw them all without exception.
The warrior maiden you seek,
A maiden who brings strife among the people,
Is fiercely venomous and full of quarrels,
And lays flat whoever grapples with her.
No one has dared approach
That forsaken, ill-starred woman.
Many giants went to claim her,
But not one remained alive.
That ill-omened maiden
Is called a girl, yet bears a lion’s fame;
No man like her exists in all the world.
The matchmaker sent to her has died,
And the shield-bearer died in peace.
Those who sought to grapple with her died;
All who journeyed there died.
Your mercilessness became your strength;
Whoever challenged you was laid low.
The valor became known
Of the doomed man who boldly rode out.
Mortals despaired of life,
And whoever faced her died.
